The first time Pooja presented Kashish's supplier analysis as her own, Kashish went home in Andheri and lay on the sofa, furious, composing speeches she would never give.
The next morning she did something duller. She opened a notes file and wrote: 3 March, supplier analysis sent to Pooja, 11:40 a.m. She started ending each week with a short progress email to the whole project group: what she had done, with the files attached.
Then she asked Pooja for coffee. "Last Thursday's supplier slides were my analysis. I'd like my name on my parts going forward." Pooja looked surprised. "I thought we were one team." "We are. I'd still like my name on my parts."
It happened once more, in April. This time Kashish took the notes file and the dated emails to her manager, and said only what had happened, in order.
The manager read them twice. "Thank you for bringing this calmly. I'll handle it."

qa.q: What did Kashish write first in the notes file?
qa.a: Kashish wrote "3 March, supplier analysis sent to Pooja, 11:40 a.m."

qa.q: What was Kashish feeling the night after the first time, and how did she handle it?
qa.a: Kashish was furious and composed angry speeches in her head, but turned that anger into careful records the next morning.

qa.q: Why did Kashish's approach work better than an angry speech?
qa.a: She kept dated records, shared progress in writing, spoke to Pooja calmly first, and only went to her manager with facts when it happened again.

qa.q: How might the manager have seen Kashish's complaint because of the way it was presented?
qa.a: The dated notes and emails, told calmly and in order, let the manager see a clear pattern instead of a personal quarrel.

grounding: Kashish keeps dated records, shares progress in writing, speaks calmly to Pooja first and takes facts to her manager when the credit-taking repeats.

"Ramesh, have you got five minutes? Just us."
"Sure, Disha. What's up?"
"In Thursday's client update, the onboarding flow was presented as yours."
"It was a team deck."
"It was. But I built the onboarding flow. Here's the document with my name and the dates, from the eighteenth to the twenty-fifth."
"...I didn't mean to take anything. I was just presenting."
"I believe that could be how it felt. But the client now thinks you designed it, and the new project was assigned to you."
"So what do you want me to do?"
"Two things. Tell the client lead that the flow was mine. And going forward, I'll present my own parts."
"That's awkward."
"A little. Less awkward than me going to our manager with this document."
Ramesh sighed. "Fine. I'll email her today and copy you."
"Thank you. That's all I needed."

qa.q: Which dates were on Disha's document?
qa.a: The dates were from the eighteenth to the twenty-fifth.

qa.q: How can you tell Disha felt calm but determined?
qa.a: Disha asked for a private chat, stuck to facts and dates, allowed that Ramesh might not have meant harm, and still clearly asked for two changes.

qa.q: What made Disha's approach a good first step before going to a manager?
qa.a: Raising it with Ramesh privately, with a dated document, gave Ramesh a chance to put it right first, while making clear that the manager was the next step.

qa.q: How might Ramesh feel about emailing the client lead?
qa.a: Ramesh finds it awkward and a bit embarrassing, but agreeing to email today and copy Disha shows Ramesh sees it is fairer than the alternative.

grounding: Disha raises a credit issue calmly with Ramesh first, backed by a dated document, and asks for a correction before involving a manager.

passage:
I'm Tejas, and last year I learnt that calm and boring beats clever and angry.
Twice, my colleague Suraj presented my test scripts as his in stand-ups. The first time, I stewed for a week and said nothing.
After the second time, I changed my habits. Every Friday I sent a short progress email to the team: what I built, with links and dates. I kept my commits clean, with my name on them. Then I asked Suraj for coffee. I didn't accuse him. I said, "In Tuesday's stand-up the login tests came across as yours. I wrote those. Can we make sure it's clear next time?" He went red and mumbled something about miscommunication.
A month later it happened again. This time I went to our manager with the emails and the commit history and said the same thing, in the same flat voice. She fixed it in the next stand-up.
I didn't have to raise my voice once.

qa.q: What did Tejas send every Friday?
qa.a: A short progress email to the team: what was built, with links and dates.

qa.q: How did Tejas feel after the first time, and how did that change?
qa.a: At first Tejas stewed silently for a week, resentful; later Tejas felt steady enough to speak in a flat, calm voice with the facts ready.

qa.q: Which steps made Tejas's case hard to dismiss?
qa.a: Dated weekly emails, a commit history with Tejas's name, a calm private talk with Suraj first, then going to the manager with the records when it repeated.

qa.q: How might Suraj have felt during the coffee conversation?
qa.a: Suraj went red and mumbled about miscommunication, probably embarrassed at being named calmly with facts he could not argue with.

grounding: Shows an employee keeping dated records, sharing progress in writing, raising credit-taking calmly first with the colleague and then the manager.

Department head's note, 3 October
Hansa from the packaging team asked for fifteen minutes today. She brought a slim folder: dated sketches, her weekly update emails to the team since July, and a note of a conversation she had with Baljeet on 19 September. In that talk she told him calmly that two of her box designs had been presented under his name at the supplier meeting, and asked that it not happen again.
It happened again last week. Baljeet's deck for the retail pitch includes her folding-tray design with no mention of her.
Hansa did not raise her voice or call him a thief. She said, "I'd like the record corrected and a clear process for credit."
What I did next: I checked the file dates against the deck. They match her account. I have scheduled a meeting with Baljeet tomorrow, asked HR to sit in, and will have her name added to the retail pitch before it goes out.

qa.q: When did Hansa first speak to Baljeet about the designs?
qa.a: On 19 September.

qa.q: What does Hansa's calm manner suggest about how she felt?
qa.a: It suggests Hansa felt steady and determined rather than furious, confident that the dated records would speak for her.

qa.q: What steps did Hansa take before going to the department head?
qa.a: She kept dated sketches and weekly update emails, and spoke calmly to Baljeet first, asking that it not happen again.

qa.q: How might Baljeet see tomorrow's meeting with HR present?
qa.a: Baljeet will likely feel exposed and uneasy, since the file dates match Hansa's account and there is little room to argue.

grounding: Shows an employee with dated records who raised credit-taking calmly with the colleague first and then with a manager when it repeated.

passage:
Wednesday
Did it. Talked to Saurabh.
For three weeks I'd kept a little log on my phone: date, what I did, who I sent it to. The budget tracker, the vendor call notes, the supplier map. All of it had turned up in Saurabh's updates to the director with only his name.
This morning I asked him for five minutes in the small meeting room. My palms were sweaty. I'd practised one sentence in the shower: "I want to talk about how my work is being credited." I said it, then showed him the log. No "you always", no "you stole".
He was quiet. Then he said he hadn't realised how it looked. I said, "From today, can we both sign the updates?" He agreed.
If it happens again, I'll take the log to Ma'am. But tonight I feel lighter than I have all month.
Vijay

qa.q: What did Vijay record in the phone log?
qa.a: Date, what Vijay did, and who it was sent to.

qa.q: How did Vijay feel before and after the talk?
qa.a: Vijay was nervous beforehand, with sweaty palms, and felt lighter afterwards than in the whole month.

qa.q: What made Vijay's talk calm and effective?
qa.a: Vijay practised one clear sentence, showed the dated log, avoided accusations like 'you stole', and asked for a concrete change: both signing the updates.

qa.q: What would change if Vijay had accused Saurabh in front of the director?
qa.a: Saurabh would likely have turned defensive, and the talk could have become a fight about tone rather than the facts in the log.

grounding: Shows an employee keeping a dated record and raising credit-taking calmly with the colleague first, with a manager as the next step.
